{{italic title}}
'''''The Strange Logic of Random Graphs''''' is a book on [[zero-one law]]s for [[random graph]]s. It was written by [[Joel Spencer]] and published in 2001 by [[Springer-Verlag]] as volume 22 of their book series [[Algorithms and Combinatorics]].

==Topics==
The random graphs of the book are generated from the [[Erdős–Rényi model|Erdős–Rényi–Gilbert model]] <math>G(n,p)</math> in which <math>n</math> vertices are given and a random choice is made whether to connect each pair of vertices by an edge, independently for each pair, with probability <math>p</math> of making a connection. A zero-one law is a theorem stating that, for certain properties of graphs, and for certain choices of <math>p</math>,
the probability of generating a graph with the property tends to zero or one in the limit as <math>n</math> goes to infinity.{{r|berarducci}}

A fundamental result in this area, proved independently by Glebskiĭ et al. and by [[Ronald Fagin]], is that there is a zero-one law for <math>G(n,1/2)</math> for every property that can be described in the [[logic of graphs|first-order logic of graphs]].{{r|kolchin}} Moreover, the limiting probability is one if and only if the infinite [[Rado graph]] has the property. For instance, a random graph in this model contains a triangle with probability tending to one; it contains a [[universal vertex]] with probability tending to zero. For other choices of <math>p</math>, other outcomes can occur.
For instance, the limiting probability of containing a triangle is between 0 and 1 when <math>p=c/n</math> for a constant <math>c</math>; it tends to 0 for smaller choices of <math>p</math> and to 1 for larger choices. The function <math>1/n</math> is said to be a ''threshold'' for the property of containing a triangle, meaning that it separates the values of <math>p</math> with limiting probability 0 from the values with limiting probability 1.{{r|berarducci}}

The main result of the book (proved by Spencer with [[Saharon Shelah]]) is that irrational powers of <math>n</math> are never threshold functions. That is, whenever <math>a>0</math> is an [[irrational number]], there is a zero-one law for the first-order properties of the random graphs <math>G(n,n^{-a})</math>.{{r|berarducci}} A key tool in the proof is the [[Ehrenfeucht–Fraïssé game]].{{r|frank}}

==Audience and reception==
Although it is essentially the proof of a single theorem, aimed at specialists in the area, the book is written in a readable style that introduces the reader to many important topics in [[finite model theory]] and the theory of random graphs. Reviewer Valentin Kolchin, himself the author of another book on random graphs, writes that the book is "self-contained, easily read, and is distinguished by elegant writing", recommending it to [[probability theory|probability theorists]] and [[mathematical logic|logicians]].{{r|kolchin}} Reviewer Alessandro Berarducci calls the book "beautifully written" and its subject "fascinating".{{r|berarducci}}
